title: Mixing Depth in Sparse Transformer FFN Layers: code, 324 training runs, and the analysis that reproduces the paper
description:
Code, raw experimental records, and analysis for a controlled study of structured sparsity in Transformer feed-forward layers under an equal-parameter and equal-FLOP constraint. Accompanies the paper Structured Sparsity in Transformer Feed-Forward Layers: Mixing Depth, and the Limits of Communication Reduction.

Seven connectivity patterns (dense, ring, small-world, random, block-diagonal, mosaic, butterfly) are compared across four densities and four depths. Per-layer coverage is shown to be an insufficient predictor of quality: two patterns with identical coverage differ by 9.6 sigma. The repository introduces the mixing depth tau — the number of layers a topology needs before every output can reach every input — computed from the binary masks alone, without training. Tau was validated with two predictions registered in the experiment scripts before the corresponding runs were queued: freezing the butterfly's stage drops its quality onto block-diagonal (landing within 0.14 sigma), and in the sparsest regime butterfly overtakes ring despite half the coverage (by 2.53 sigma). Two bounds are established on what sparse sharding can save in distributed training: an information-theoretic one and a latency floor that reducing bytes cannot cross.

Contents: the polytopo package (topology constructors, coverage and mixing-depth computation, GPT-mini with a pluggable FFN), 324 raw training-run records and 10 communication and latency measurements as JSON, the SLURM scripts documenting every experimental grid, and analysis code that recomputes every number in the paper from the raw records — no value in any table or figure is hand-entered. Records that must not be analysed (runs from an older code version, exact duplicates, smoke tests) are segregated with the reason stated, because nothing in their recorded arguments distinguishes them from valid runs.

All runs were performed at TUBITAK ULAKBIM TRUBA: the layer-scale study on an NVIDIA A100, everything else on NVIDIA H200s.
